subject: Surgery
title: Principles of Surgical Infection and Infection Control

source.title: Principles of Surgical Infection and Infection Control

objectives: Recommend patient and surgeon measures that minimise surgical site infection.
State the indications, timing and duration of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis.
Manage an established surgical wound infection, including when to add antibiotics.
Select an antibiotic from patient factors and the likely organism.
Classify the main antibiotic classes by spectrum and key toxicity.
Apply standard precautions, safe sharps handling and hand hygiene.
Distinguish cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation and choose the right method.

sections.title: Reducing SSI: patient & surgeon
sections.digest: Surgical site infection (**SSI**) is minimised by optimising the **patient**, the **surgeon** and the environment. Patient factors: correct predisposing conditions (control **diabetes**, stop smoking, correct nutritional deficiency), avoid operating during active infection, **clip rather than shave** hair just before incision (shaving causes micro-abrasions that colonise), and prepare the skin with antiseptic. Surgeon factors: short nails and proper scrubbing; meticulous technique with adequate **haemostasis**, gentle tissue handling, and avoidance of tight sutures or **dead space**; and delayed primary closure of heavily contaminated wounds.
highYield: Clip, do not shave — shaving causes colonisable micro-abrasions.
Control diabetes, stop smoking and correct nutrition before elective surgery.
Good technique: haemostasis, gentle handling, no dead space or tight sutures.
Heavily contaminated wound → delayed primary closure.

tables.title: Reducing surgical site infection
rows: Control diabetes, stop smoking, correct nutrition
Clip (not shave) hair just before incision
Avoid tight sutures and dead space
Delayed primary closure of dirty wounds

pitfalls: Shaving the night before increases infection — clip immediately before incision instead.

sections.title: Prophylactic antibiotics
sections.digest: **Prophylactic antibiotics** are a brief course just before an operation to reduce organisms below the level that overcomes host defences. Indications: in **clean surgery** only when prosthetic material is implanted or the patient is high-risk (elderly, obese, smoker, immunocompromised); in **all contaminated classes** (clean-contaminated, contaminated, dirty). The antibiotic is given about **one hour before** incision, with a booster in long operations; prophylaxis should **not exceed one day**. A first-generation cephalosporin (**cefazolin/cephazolin**) is usual, but each hospital's infection-control committee may recommend an agent for its prevalent organism (e.g. **ampicillin-sulbactam**).
highYield: Give prophylaxis ~1 hour before incision; do not continue beyond one day.
Clean surgery: prophylaxis only for prosthesis or high-risk patient.
All contaminated classes get prophylaxis.
Cefazolin or ampicillin-sulbactam are typical choices.

tables.title: Prophylaxis indications
rows: Only if prosthesis implanted or high-risk patient

pitfalls: Prophylaxis is not treatment — do not continue it beyond one day.
Timing matters: give it about an hour before incision, not after.

sections.title: Treatment of established SSI
sections.digest: Established SSI is treated first by **liberal drainage** — open the wound by removing skin stitches. **Antibiotics** are added only if there is evidence of **invasive infection**: temperature **>38.5°C**, erythema **>5 cm**, or leucocyte count **>11,000**. Guide antibiotic choice by **culture and sensitivity**, and trace and correct any source of hospital-acquired infection. The treatment of an **abscess** is drainage; the treatment of a spreading infection (cellulitis) is antibiotics.
highYield: Treat an established wound infection first by opening it (drainage).
Add antibiotics only for invasive infection: T >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, or WBC >11,000.
Abscess → drainage; spreading infection → antibiotics.
Guide antibiotics by culture and sensitivity.
pitfalls: An abscess needs drainage, not just antibiotics — antibiotics alone will not cure a collection.

sections.title: Choosing an antibiotic
sections.digest: Before starting therapy, weigh the **patient** and the **likely organism**. Patient factors: allergy, age, renal/hepatic function, host resistance (compromised by recent hospitalisation or antibiotics in the last 90 days), ability to take oral drugs, pregnancy/lactation, and the organism's sensitivity. Principles: send relevant **culture and sensitivity** (urine, sputum, pus) early; choose an agent effective against the likely pathogen while avoiding needlessly toxic or costly drugs; judge course length by the pathology and clinical/laboratory response, avoiding prolonged courses; change agents based on culture **and** clinical response — do not switch for culture results alone if the patient is responding.
highYield: Send culture and sensitivity early, before or as therapy starts.
Recent hospitalisation or antibiotics (90 days) implies a resistant flora.
Do not change a working antibiotic for culture results alone.
pitfalls: A satisfactory clinical response outweighs a discordant culture — do not switch needlessly.

sections.title: Antibiotic classes
sections.digest: **Beta-lactams** inhibit cell-wall synthesis. **Penicillins:** penicillin G (Gram-positives, spirochaetes); semisynthetic (methicillin) for staph/strep; ampicillin (enterococci, some Gram-negatives); amoxicillin + a **beta-lactamase inhibitor** (clavulanate) broadens cover. **Cephalosporins:** 1st gen (cefazolin, cephalexin) strong Gram-positive; 2nd gen (cefuroxime, cefoxitin) better Gram-negative, some anaerobic; 3rd gen (ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefotaxime) strong Gram-negative, variable Gram-positive; 4th gen (cefepime). **Carbapenems** (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) are broadest. **Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) hit Gram-negative aerobes but are oto- and nephrotoxic — a last resort, monitored by levels. **Quinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) target Gram-negative aerobes (UTIs). **Glycopeptides** (**vancomycin**) cover Gram-positives including **MRSA** and are the drug of choice for **Clostridioides difficile** colitis. **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole** covers Gram-negatives and Pneumocystis/Nocardia. **Macrolides** (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin) cover Gram-positives and suit beta-lactam-allergic patients.
highYield: Vancomycin: MRSA and C. difficile colitis drug of choice.
Aminoglycosides: Gram-negative aerobes, oto/nephrotoxic — monitor and limit.
Cephalosporin trend: Gram-positive cover falls and Gram-negative rises across generations.
Carbapenems are the broadest-spectrum beta-lactams.
Add a beta-lactamase inhibitor (clavulanate/sulbactam) to broaden a penicillin.
pitfalls: MRSA is resistant to all first-generation cephalosporins — use vancomycin.
Aminoglycosides are a last resort; prefer safer 3rd-gen cephalosporins/quinolones where possible.

sections.title: Complications of antibiotics
sections.digest: Antibiotic complications: **hypersensitivity** (common with penicillin/streptomycin — urticaria, fever, angioneurotic oedema, asthma, rarely anaphylaxis); **vitamin B deficiency** from altered bowel flora with prolonged use; **superinfection** with resistant strains (Proteus, Pseudomonas, Candida) affecting mouth, bowel, urinary tract or lung; and **specific toxicities** such as the nephro- and ototoxicity of aminoglycosides. Prolonged broad-spectrum use also risks **Clostridioides difficile** colitis.
highYield: Penicillin/streptomycin → hypersensitivity, rarely anaphylaxis.
Aminoglycosides → nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Broad-spectrum use → superinfection and C. difficile colitis.
pitfalls: A history of penicillin anaphylaxis contraindicates the drug — do not re-challenge casually.

sections.title: Standard precautions
sections.digest: **Nosocomial** infections are acquired in hospital. **Standard precautions** prevent transmission via blood, body fluids, non-intact skin and mucosa, and are used for every patient regardless of status. **Hand hygiene** (soap-and-water or alcohol gel) is the single most effective measure and is done before/after patient contact and after touching fluids/contaminated items even when gloved. **PPE:** gloves for contact with fluids/non-intact skin; mask, gown and goggles when splash is likely. **Sharps:** never recap used needles; discard immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container. **Safe injection:** new needle and syringe for each access and each patient. For hepatitis/HIV, add double gloves, full-face mask, eye protection, waterproof gowns, and pass sharps indirectly in a kidney basin.
highYield: Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure against hospital-acquired infection.
Never recap needles; discard into a puncture-resistant sharps container.
Perform hand hygiene even when gloves were worn.
For hepatitis/HIV surgery: double gloves, eye protection, indirect sharps passing.
pitfalls: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene — wash/gel after removing them.
Recapping needles is a classic cause of needle-stick injury — do not do it.

sections.title: Decontamination & sterilisation
sections.digest: **Decontamination** removes microbial contaminants by cleaning, disinfection or sterilisation. **Cleaning** removes visible soil and is a prerequisite — most disinfectants fail in the presence of organic matter. **Disinfection** reduces viable organisms to acceptable levels: **antiseptics** are disinfectants safe on tissue (chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, alcohol, hexachlorophene); moist heat (boiling) or chemical agents such as **glutaraldehyde (Cidex)** disinfect heat-sensitive endoscopes (rinse with sterile saline afterwards as it is toxic). **Sterilisation** destroys all organisms including spores; the standard is **steam autoclaving at 134°C, 2 atmospheres for 20–30 minutes**. Alternatives: **ethylene oxide** for heat-sensitive items, glutaraldehyde with long immersion, gamma irradiation (industrial), and gas plasma (delicate catheters/wires).
highYield: Clean before you disinfect — organic matter inactivates disinfectants.
Autoclave standard: 134°C, 2 atmospheres, 20–30 minutes.
Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) disinfects endoscopes; rinse with sterile saline (toxic).
Ethylene oxide/gamma/gas plasma sterilise heat-sensitive items.

tables.title: Common antiseptics
rows: Skin prep, handwash, open wounds; broad Gram +/−

pitfalls: Disinfection is not sterilisation — spores survive disinfection.
Rinse glutaraldehyde-treated scopes with sterile saline before use; the agent is toxic.

cards.front: Why is clipping preferred to shaving before surgery?
cards.back: Shaving causes micro-abrasions that become colonised by bacteria; clipping avoids this.

cards.front: Name three patient factors to correct before elective surgery.
cards.back: Control diabetes, stop smoking and correct nutritional deficiency.

cards.cloze: Hair should be removed by {{c1::clipping}} just before skin incision, not by shaving.

cards.front: Name three elements of meticulous surgical technique that reduce SSI.
cards.back: Adequate haemostasis, gentle tissue handling, and avoiding tight sutures or dead space.

cards.front: How is a heavily contaminated wound best closed to reduce infection?
cards.back: By delayed primary closure.

cards.front: Should elective surgery proceed during an active infection?
cards.back: No — avoid operating in patients with active infection where possible.

cards.front: What are prophylactic antibiotics for?
cards.back: A brief pre-operative course to reduce organisms below the level that overcomes host defences.

cards.cloze: The prophylactic antibiotic is given about {{c1::one hour}} before surgery.

cards.front: How long may surgical antibiotic prophylaxis continue?
cards.back: It should not exceed one day.

cards.front: When is prophylaxis indicated in clean surgery?
cards.back: Only when prosthetic material is implanted or the patient is high-risk (elderly, obese, smoker, immunocompromised).

cards.front: Which wound classes always receive prophylaxis?
cards.back: All contaminated classes: clean-contaminated, contaminated and dirty.

cards.front: Which antibiotics are typical first choices for prophylaxis?
cards.back: A first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin) or ampicillin-sulbactam.

cards.front: Maximum duration of surgical prophylaxis (in days).
What is the first treatment of an established wound infection?
cards.back: Liberal drainage — open the wound by removing skin stitches.

cards.front: When are antibiotics added to a drained wound infection?
cards.back: Only with evidence of invasive infection: temperature >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, or WBC >11,000.

cards.cloze: Invasive infection is suggested by erythema more than {{c1::5}} cm around the wound.

cards.front: What treats an abscess versus a spreading infection?
cards.back: An abscess needs drainage; a spreading infection needs antibiotics.

cards.front: What should guide antibiotic choice in SSI?
cards.back: Culture and sensitivity tests.

cards.front: Which recent factors imply the host may harbour resistant organisms?
cards.back: Previous hospitalisation or antibiotic therapy within the last 90 days.

cards.front: What samples are sent early when managing SSI?
cards.back: Relevant culture and sensitivity samples (urine, sputum or pus).

cards.front: Should you change a working antibiotic because of a discordant culture result?
cards.back: No — if there is a satisfactory clinical response, do not change for culture alone.

cards.cloze: Patient factors in antibiotic choice include allergy, age, renal/hepatic function and {{c1::pregnancy/lactation}}.

cards.front: How do beta-lactam antibiotics work?
cards.back: They inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, causing cell lysis.

cards.cloze: Adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as {{c1::clavulanate}} broadens amoxicillin's spectrum.

cards.front: How does cephalosporin spectrum change across generations?
cards.back: Gram-positive cover falls while Gram-negative cover rises (1st → 3rd/4th).

cards.front: Give a first-generation cephalosporin used in surgery.
cards.back: Cefazolin (or cephalexin).

cards.front: Which class has the broadest spectrum, covering Pseudomonas and anaerobes?
cards.back: Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem).

cards.front: Two major toxicities of aminoglycosides?
cards.back: Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

cards.front: What is vancomycin the drug of choice for?
cards.back: MRSA and Clostridioides difficile colitis.

cards.cloze: Vancomycin is a {{c1::glycopeptide}} active against MRSA.

cards.front: Common clinical use of quinolones?
cards.back: Urinary tract infections (Gram-negative aerobes).

cards.front: When are macrolides especially useful?
cards.back: In patients allergic to beta-lactam agents (they cover Gram-positives).

cards.front: Which unusual organisms does trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole cover?
cards.back: Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) and Nocardia.

cards.front: Drug of choice for C. difficile colitis (one word).
cards.back: vancomycin

cards.front: Which antibiotics classically cause hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Penicillin and streptomycin (urticaria, angioneurotic oedema, rarely anaphylaxis).

cards.front: Which organisms typically cause superinfection?
cards.back: Resistant strains such as Proteus, Pseudomonas or Candida.

cards.cloze: Prolonged antibiotics cause {{c1::vitamin B}} deficiency by altering bowel flora.

cards.front: Which class is noted for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity?
cards.back: Aminoglycosides.

cards.front: What is the single most effective measure against hospital-acquired infection?
cards.back: Proper hand hygiene.

cards.cloze: Hand hygiene is performed even when {{c1::gloves}} were worn during contact.

cards.front: How should used needles be handled?
cards.back: Discarded immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container, never recapped or removed from the syringe.

cards.front: When are mask, gown and goggles used?
cards.back: When there is a reasonable chance of a splash or spray of blood or body fluids.

cards.front: Name three extra precautions when operating on hepatitis/HIV patients.
cards.back: Double gloves, eye protection and passing sharps indirectly in a kidney basin (also full-face mask, waterproof gowns).

cards.front: Define a nosocomial infection.
cards.back: An infection acquired in hospital.

cards.front: Why must cleaning precede disinfection?
cards.back: Most disinfectants are inactivated by dirt and organic matter.

cards.front: State the standard autoclave parameters.
cards.back: Steam at 134°C and 2 atmospheres for 20–30 minutes.

cards.cloze: {{c1::Ethylene oxide}} gas is used to sterilise heat-sensitive equipment.

cards.front: Which agent disinfects endoscopes, and what is done afterwards?
cards.back: Glutaraldehyde (Cidex); rinse with sterile saline before use as it is toxic.

cards.front: Name two antiseptics used for skin preparation.
cards.back: Chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine (also 70% alcohol).

cards.front: What distinguishes sterilisation from disinfection?
cards.back: Sterilisation destroys all organisms including spores; disinfection only reduces viable organisms.

cards.front: What skin measure precedes incision?
cards.back: Skin preparation with an antiseptic.

cards.cloze: The surgeon should have short nails and should {{c1::scrub}} properly.

cards.front: Why avoid leaving dead space in a wound?
cards.back: Dead space collects fluid/haematoma that predisposes to infection.

cards.front: When is a booster prophylactic dose given?
cards.back: During a lengthy operation; further doses depend on contamination.

cards.front: Give two high-risk patient features that justify clean-case prophylaxis.
cards.back: Old age, obesity, smoking or immunocompromise.

cards.cloze: A hospital's {{c1::infection-control committee}} recommends the prophylactic agent for its prevalent organism.

cards.front: Give the three thresholds defining invasive wound infection.
cards.back: Temperature >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, and leucocyte count >11,000.

cards.front: Besides local care, what must be done about hospital-acquired infection?
cards.back: Trace and correct its source.

cards.cloze: An established wound infection is opened by removing the {{c1::skin stitches}}.

cards.front: How is the length of an antibiotic course judged?
cards.back: By the pathology and the clinical and laboratory assessment; avoid prolonged courses.

cards.front: Why avoid toxic or very costly antibiotics?
cards.back: Because an equally effective, safer or cheaper substitute is usually available.

cards.front: Prototype penicillin and its main spectrum?
cards.back: Penicillin G — mainly Gram-positives such as streptococci and spirochaetes.

cards.front: What does ampicillin add over penicillin G?
cards.back: Activity against enterococci and some Gram-negative bacteria.

cards.cloze: Second-generation cephalosporins such as {{c1::cefoxitin}} also cover some anaerobes.

cards.front: Name a third-generation cephalosporin.
cards.back: Ceftriaxone, ceftazidime or cefotaxime.

cards.front: Name the fourth-generation cephalosporin mentioned.
cards.back: Cefepime.

cards.front: Name three aminoglycosides.
cards.back: Gentamicin, tobramycin and amikacin.

cards.front: How is aminoglycoside toxicity monitored?
cards.back: By serum creatinine and drug levels; use is limited and controlled.

cards.front: Name three macrolides.
cards.back: Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin.

cards.front: Give the common name for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
cards.back: Septrin (co-trimoxazole).

cards.cloze: Beta-lactams cause bacterial {{c1::cell lysis}} by blocking cell-wall synthesis.

cards.front: List features of antibiotic hypersensitivity.
cards.back: Urticaria, fever, angioneurotic oedema, asthma and rarely anaphylaxis.

cards.front: Which sites are commonly affected by superinfection?
cards.back: Mouth, bowel, urinary tract or lung.

cards.front: When should gloves be worn?
cards.back: When touching blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, mucous membranes or contaminated items.

cards.front: State two safe injection practices.
cards.back: New needle/syringe for each vial or IV-bag access and for each patient; single-patient vials where possible.

cards.cloze: Used sharps go into a leak-proof, {{c1::puncture-resistant}} container.

cards.front: Name the three methods of decontamination.
cards.back: Cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation.

cards.front: Which antiseptic is fast-acting and usable on open wounds?
cards.back: Povidone-iodine (effective against Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms).

cards.cloze: The standard autoclave attains {{c1::134}}°C at 2 atmospheres.

cards.front: Which sterilisation method suits delicate endovascular wires in hospital?
cards.back: Gas plasma.

cards.front: Which cocci, besides MRSA, does vancomycin cover?
cards.back: Anaerobic Gram-positive cocci such as enterococci.

cards.front: Why avoid tight sutures?
cards.back: They cause ischaemia, increasing infection and impairing healing.

cards.front: What is the treatment of a spreading (non-collected) infection?
cards.back: Antibiotics.

cards.front: Which colitis follows overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile?
cards.back: Antibiotic-associated (pseudomembranous) colitis; vancomycin is a treatment.

cards.front: What is the aim of prophylaxis in terms of organisms?
cards.back: To reduce organisms below the level that can overcome host defences.

cards.front: What routes do standard precautions target?
cards.back: Blood, body fluids, non-intact skin and mucous membranes.

cards.front: What is disinfection by moist heat?
cards.back: Boiling water.

cards.front: Name three quinolones.
cards.back: Norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.

cards.front: Which samples are most useful for culture in SSI?
cards.back: Urine, sputum or pus.

cards.front: What determines whether further prophylactic doses are given?
cards.back: The degree of wound contamination during the operation.

cards.front: Are MRSA strains sensitive to first-generation cephalosporins?
cards.back: No — methicillin-resistant strains are invariably resistant to them.

mcqs.stem: Which method of pre-operative hair removal carries the lowest infection risk?

options.why: Increases infection via micro-abrasions colonised overnight.
Removal is sometimes needed; the question is the method.

explanation: Shaving causes micro-abrasions that colonise.
Clipping immediately before incision is preferred.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Choose the least traumatic hair removal.

mcqs.stem: Prophylactic antibiotics for a clean operation are indicated when:

options.why: Clean cases usually do not need prophylaxis.

options.text: A prosthesis is implanted or the patient is high-risk

options.why: Duration alone is not the indication.

options.text: Only if the patient requests it

explanation: Clean surgery generally needs no prophylaxis.
Exceptions are prosthetic implantation or a high-risk patient.
keyFacts: Clean case prophylaxis: prosthesis or high-risk only.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Reserve clean-case prophylaxis for clear indications.

mcqs.stem: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is best given:

options.why: Too early to be effective at incision.

options.text: At the end of the operation

options.why: Prophylaxis should not exceed one day.

options.text: Only if the wound looks dirty afterwards

explanation: Tissue levels must be adequate at incision.
Give the dose about an hour before, not continued beyond one day.

mcqs.stem: A drained wound infection now has a temperature of 39°C, spreading erythema of 7 cm and WBC 14,000. The correct addition is:

options.why: Invasive signs are present, warranting antibiotics.

options.text: Add antibiotics guided by culture and sensitivity

options.why: Do not close an infected wound.

options.text: Give prophylactic antibiotics for five days

explanation: Invasive infection is defined by T >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, or WBC >11,000.
All are met, so add culture-guided antibiotics.

mcqs.stem: The correct primary treatment of a wound abscess is:

options.why: Antibiotics cannot clear a collection alone.
Do not close an abscess cavity.

explanation: An abscess is a localised collection.
The treatment is drainage; antibiotics treat spreading infection.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Drain collections; do not just prescribe.

mcqs.stem: A patient develops a wound infection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The most appropriate antibiotic is:

options.why: MRSA is resistant to first-generation cephalosporins.
Not the drug of choice for MRSA.

explanation: MRSA resists beta-lactams including cephalosporins.
Vancomycin, a glycopeptide, is the appropriate choice.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match resistant organisms to their agents.

mcqs.stem: Which antibiotic is the drug of choice for antibiotic-associated Clostridioides difficile colitis?

options.why: Not effective for C. difficile colitis.
A cephalosporin can precipitate C. difficile.

explanation: C. difficile overgrows after broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oral vancomycin is a drug of choice (with metronidazole).
mcqs.teachingPoint: Treat the colitis, stop the offending drug.

mcqs.stem: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are best described as:

options.text: Gram-negative agents that are oto- and nephrotoxic

explanation: Aminoglycosides target Gram-negative aerobes.
They are oto- and nephrotoxic, so are limited and monitored.

mcqs.stem: Across cephalosporin generations, the general trend is:

options.text: Loss of all activity by the third generation
options.why: Third-generation agents are potent Gram-negative drugs.

explanation: First-generation cephalosporins are best against Gram-positives.
Later generations gain Gram-negative cover and lose some Gram-positive.
keyFacts: Higher generation → more Gram-negative, less Gram-positive.

mcqs.stem: The single most effective measure to reduce hospital-acquired infection is:

options.why: Useful but not the most effective single measure.

options.text: Wearing a mask at all times
options.why: Not the single most effective measure.
Not feasible or the key measure.

explanation: Hand hygiene interrupts transmission between patients.
It is the single most effective infection-control measure.

mcqs.stem: Which practice increases the risk of a needle-stick injury?

options.why: Correct — recapping is a classic cause.

options.text: Passing sharps in a kidney basin
Using a new needle per patient

explanation: Used needles must be discarded, not recapped.
Recapping is a classic cause of needle-stick injury.

mcqs.stem: Which is the standard method of sterilisation in a hospital?

options.why: Boiling disinfects but does not sterilise spores.

explanation: Sterilisation destroys all organisms including spores.
The standard is steam autoclaving (134°C, 2 atm, 20–30 min).

mcqs.stem: Why must instruments be cleaned before disinfection?

options.why: The reason is microbiological, not cosmetic.

options.text: Because organic matter inactivates most disinfectants
Because disinfectants are cheaper on clean items

explanation: Most disinfectants fail in the presence of dirt/organic matter.
Cleaning is therefore a prerequisite.

mcqs.stem: After chemical disinfection of an endoscope with glutaraldehyde, the scope should be:

options.why: The agent is toxic and must be rinsed off.

options.text: Rinsed with sterile saline before use
Left to air-dry for a week

explanation: Glutaraldehyde is toxic to tissue.
Scopes are rinsed with sterile saline before use.
keyFacts: Rinse glutaraldehyde scopes with sterile saline.

mcqs.stem: A patient given prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics develops profuse diarrhoea. The most likely cause is:

options.why: Occurs but does not usually cause profuse diarrhoea.
Less likely given the antibiotic history.

explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics disturb bowel flora.
C. difficile overgrowth causes antibiotic-associated colitis.

mcqs.stem: Which agent broadens a penicillin's spectrum by inhibiting beta-lactamase?

options.why: An anaerobic agent, not a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

explanation: Beta-lactamase inhibitors protect the penicillin ring.
Clavulanate broadens amoxicillin's spectrum.

mcqs.stem: A patient responding well clinically has a culture suggesting a different antibiotic. You should:

options.text: Switch immediately to match the culture
options.why: Do not switch for culture alone if responding.
Not indicated by the culture alone.

explanation: Culture guides but does not override a good clinical response.
Do not change a working antibiotic for culture results alone.
keyFacts: Treat the patient, not the culture.

mcqs.stem: Which class is most appropriate for a straightforward Gram-negative urinary tract infection?
explanation: Quinolones target Gram-negative aerobes.
They are commonly used for urinary tract infections.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match the class to the site/organism.

mcqs.stem: Which surgical technique factor reduces surgical site infection?

options.why: Tight sutures cause ischaemia and infection.

explanation: Good technique minimises trauma, haematoma and dead space.
This reduces infection risk.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Technique is part of infection control.

mcqs.stem: Which antibiotic class most classically causes hypersensitivity reactions?

options.why: Noted for oto/nephrotoxicity, not classic hypersensitivity.
Cause 'red man' with rapid infusion, but penicillin is the classic allergen.

explanation: Penicillins (and streptomycin) classically cause hypersensitivity.
Reactions range from urticaria to anaphylaxis.

mcqs.stem: Which is a correct principle of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Continue for a week to be safe
options.why: Prophylaxis should not exceed one day.

options.text: Give it about an hour before incision
Only start it if infection appears
Use the most toxic agent available

explanation: Adequate tissue levels are needed at incision.
Give ~1 h before and do not exceed one day.
keyFacts: Right drug, right time, short course.

mcqs.stem: Standard precautions should be applied to:

options.text: Only patients known to be infectious
All patients regardless of infection status

explanation: Standard precautions assume any patient may transmit infection.
They are used for everyone, infectious or not.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Treat every patient as potentially infectious.

mcqs.stem: Which sterilisation method is most appropriate for heat-sensitive equipment?
explanation: Heat-sensitive items cannot be autoclaved.
Ethylene oxide gas sterilises them (gamma/gas plasma also).

mcqs.stem: Which statement about vancomycin is correct?

options.text: It is a cell-membrane channel blocker
It is effective against MRSA and Gram-positive cocci
It is a first-line Gram-negative agent
It is used mainly for urinary infections

explanation: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide inhibiting cell-wall synthesis.
It covers MRSA and Gram-positive cocci and treats C. difficile colitis.

mcqs.stem: Antibiotics are indicated in a wound infection when which threshold is met?

options.why: Minor erythema alone does not define invasion.
Correct — one of the invasive-infection criteria.

explanation: Invasive infection: T >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, or WBC >11,000.
Erythema >5 cm meets the criterion.

mcqs.stem: Which organism produces coagulase and tends to localise infection with pus formation?
explanation: Staphylococci produce coagulase.
This localises infection and produces pus.

mcqs.stem: Disinfection differs from sterilisation in that disinfection:

options.text: Reduces organisms but may not kill spores
Is unnecessary if cleaning is done

options.why: Disinfection reduces, not necessarily eliminates all.

explanation: Disinfection lowers viable organisms to acceptable levels.
Spores can survive; sterilisation destroys them.
keyFacts: Disinfection spares spores; sterilisation does not.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Choose the level to the risk.

mcqs.stem: Which is a specific toxicity of aminoglycosides to warn about?
explanation: Aminoglycosides accumulate in kidney and inner ear.
They cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

mcqs.stem: Which patient factor most suggests a resistant organism when choosing empirical antibiotics?

options.text: Antibiotic therapy within the last 90 days

explanation: Recent antibiotics or hospitalisation select resistant flora.
This compromises host resistance and guides broader empirical cover.

mcqs.stem: Which is a correct patient-side measure to reduce SSI?

options.text: Shave the operative site the night before
Control diabetes and stop smoking pre-operatively
Operate through active infection to save time
Skip skin antisepsis if the skin looks clean
Leave dead space to reduce operating time

explanation: Optimising the patient lowers infection risk.
Control diabetes, stop smoking and correct nutrition first.
keyFacts: Prepare the patient before elective surgery.

mcqs.stem: Which antibiotic is effective against Pseudomonas and anaerobes as a broad agent?

options.why: A quinolone, not the broadest agent.

explanation: Carbapenems are the broadest beta-lactams.
Meropenem covers Pseudomonas and anaerobes.

mcqs.stem: Prolonged antibiotics can cause vitamin B deficiency because they:

options.text: Alter bowel flora that synthesise vitamins

explanation: Gut flora contribute to vitamin synthesis.
Prolonged antibiotics disturb this, causing vitamin B deficiency.
keyFacts: Antibiotics + flora loss → vitamin B deficiency.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Consider flora effects of long courses.

mcqs.stem: When should hand hygiene be performed relative to glove use?

options.text: Only if gloves were not worn
options.why: Perform it even when gloves were worn.

options.text: Before and after patient contact, including after glove removal

options.why: It is routine, not only when soiled.

options.text: Never, if alcohol gel is unavailable
options.why: Soap and water is an alternative.

explanation: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
Perform it before/after contact and after removing gloves.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Gloves plus hand hygiene, not either alone.

mcqs.stem: Which agent is a topical disinfectant safe to apply to tissue?
explanation: Antiseptics are disinfectants safe on epithelial tissue.
Chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine are examples.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Do not confuse antiseptics with steriliser chemicals.

mcqs.stem: How long should surgical antibiotic prophylaxis usually continue?
explanation: Prophylaxis reduces peri-operative contamination.
It should not exceed one day.

mcqs.stem: A penicillin-allergic patient needs cover for a Gram-positive infection. A reasonable choice is:

options.why: Some cross-reactivity risk; not the described first choice for allergy.

explanation: Macrolides cover Gram-positives.
They are used when beta-lactams are contraindicated by allergy.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about abscess management is correct?

options.why: Do not close an abscess cavity.

options.text: It never needs antibiotics even if invasive
options.why: Antibiotics are added for invasive signs.

explanation: An abscess is a localised pus collection.
Drainage is primary; antibiotics are for spreading/invasive infection.

mcqs.stem: Delayed primary closure is most appropriate for a:

options.text: Simple surgical wound with good haemostasis

explanation: Heavily contaminated wounds risk infection if closed at once.
Delayed primary closure reduces this risk.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Delay closure when contamination is high.

mcqs.stem: Which class inhibits bacterial protein synthesis rather than the cell wall?
explanation: Beta-lactams and glycopeptides act on the cell wall.
Aminoglycosides interfere with protein synthesis.

mcqs.stem: The correct order of decontamination when organic soil is present is:
explanation: Organic matter inactivates disinfectants.
Clean first, then disinfect or sterilise.

mcqs.stem: Which is a correct safe-injection practice?

options.text: Reuse a needle between patients if wiped
Use a new needle and syringe for each patient
Access multiple patients from one vial freely
Share syringes if the needle is changed

explanation: Bloodborne outbreaks prompted stricter injection rules.
Use a new needle and syringe for each access and each patient.

mcqs.stem: Which is a recognised complication of antibiotic therapy?
explanation: Antibiotics can select resistant strains.
Superinfection with Proteus, Pseudomonas or Candida may follow.

mcqs.stem: Before starting antibiotic therapy for SSI, the surgeon should primarily consider:

options.text: The patient status and the likely organism

options.why: Not without considering the likely pathogen.

explanation: Rational prescribing weighs host and organism.
Consider patient status and the most likely causative organism.

mcqs.stem: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is preferred over amoxicillin because clavulanate:

options.why: It inhibits an enzyme, not a direct killer.
It broadens across Gram +/− and some anaerobes.

explanation: Beta-lactamase inactivates plain amoxicillin.
Clavulanate inhibits the enzyme, restoring and broadening activity.

mcqs.stem: Which finding would justify adding antibiotics to a drained wound infection?

options.text: A small amount of serous ooze

explanation: Invasive criteria: T >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, WBC >11,000.
A WBC of 14,000 meets one criterion.

mcqs.stem: Which is true of ethylene oxide?

options.text: It is the standard method for heat-stable steel

explanation: Heat-sensitive items cannot be autoclaved.
Ethylene oxide gas sterilises them.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Pick the steriliser for the material.

emqs.instruction: For each clinical situation, select the single most appropriate antibiotic.

stems.stem: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for a clean orthopaedic implant.
stems.why: A first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin) is standard prophylaxis.

stems.stem: An uncomplicated Gram-negative urinary tract infection.
stems.why: A quinolone targets Gram-negative urinary pathogens.

stems.stem: A Gram-positive infection in a patient with severe penicillin allergy.
stems.why: A macrolide is used when beta-lactams are contraindicated.

emqs.instruction: For each requirement, select the single most appropriate method.

stems.stem: Sterilising a heat-stable stainless-steel instrument set.
stems.why: Steam autoclaving is the standard for heat-stable items.

stems.stem: Sterilising heat-sensitive electronic equipment in hospital.
Chemical disinfection of a flexible endoscope.
Industrial-scale sterilisation of pre-packed catheters and syringes.

emqs.instruction: For each scenario, select the single best next step.

stems.stem: An established wound infection with intact stitches and pus beneath.
stems.why: Liberal drainage by removing stitches is the first step.

stems.stem: A drained infection now with T 39°C, erythema 8 cm and WBC 13,000.
A heavily contaminated traumatic wound at the end of debridement.
stems.why: Delayed primary closure is used for heavily contaminated wounds.

stems.stem: Profuse diarrhoea after prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics.
stems.why: This suggests C. difficile colitis, treated with vancomycin.

emqs.instruction: For each description, select the single best-matching class.

stems.stem: Inhibit cell-wall synthesis and include penicillins and cephalosporins.
Effective Gram-negative agents limited by oto- and nephrotoxicity.
Broadest beta-lactams covering Pseudomonas and anaerobes.
Cover MRSA and treat Clostridioides difficile colitis.
stems.why: Glycopeptides (vancomycin) cover MRSA and C. difficile.

summary: Minimise SSI by optimising the patient (control diabetes, stop smoking, clip not shave, antiseptic prep) and surgeon (scrub, haemostasis, gentle handling, no dead space, delayed closure of dirty wounds). Give prophylaxis about an hour before incision for prosthetic or high-risk clean cases and all contaminated classes, not beyond one day (cefazolin or ampicillin-sulbactam). Treat an established infection first by drainage, adding culture-guided antibiotics only for invasive signs (T >38.5°C, erythema >5 cm, WBC >11,000); drain an abscess, give antibiotics for spreading infection. Know the antibiotic classes — beta-lactams, cephalosporin generations, carbapenems, toxic aminoglycosides, quinolones for Gram-negative UTIs, vancomycin for MRSA and C. difficile, macrolides for penicillin allergy — and their complications. Hand hygiene is the single most effective precaution; never recap needles; and remember the decontamination ladder from cleaning through disinfection to autoclave sterilisation (134°C, 2 atm, 20–30 min).
